nameStory: Araneus bonsallae is named after someone named Bonsall, following the scientific tradition of honoring researchers who contributed to spider knowledge. Since this species lacks a widely-used common name, it's typically referred to by its scientific name in the field guides.
description: Araneus bonsallae is an orb weaver spider that builds the classic circular webs we often associate with Halloween decorations. Like other members of the Araneus genus, it has a rounded abdomen and builds geometric webs to catch flying insects. This species is quite rare in New England, with only a handful of confirmed sightings, making it a special find for any spider enthusiast. Based on its relatives, it likely has the typical orb weaver body plan with a bulbous abdomen and relatively short legs.

idTips.label: Web
idTips.description: Builds a classic circular orb web with radiating spokes and spiral capture threads that feel slightly sticky to the touch when accidentally walked into

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Round, bulbous abdomen that feels firm but slightly yielding if gently touched, with a smaller oval cephalothorax (front body section)

idTips.label: Behavior
idTips.description: Often sits in the center of its web or hides nearby, quickly running to vibrating prey with a characteristic bouncing motion that makes the whole web shake

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Medium-sized orb weaver, likely with a body length similar to other Araneus species, fitting comfortably on a quarter

habitat: Given its extreme rarity in New England with only 4 recorded observations, specific habitat preferences are unclear in our region. Based on its Texas origins, it may prefer warmer microclimates like south-facing slopes or areas near buildings that provide extra warmth. Look for orb webs in gardens, forest edges, or brushy areas where flying insects are abundant.

seasonality.spring: Adults may begin appearing as temperatures warm, starting to build their first webs of the season in protected spots.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be found in their webs, actively hunting and potentially mating.
seasonality.fall: May still be active into early fall, with females possibly creating egg sacs before the first frost.
seasonality.winter: Likely overwinters as eggs or juveniles in protected locations, with adults dying off after the first hard freeze.

funFact: This spider is so rare in New England that you're more likely to spot a shooting star than find one of these orb weavers - with only 4 confirmed sightings in the entire region, discovering one would make you part of a very exclusive club of observers!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with other Araneus orb weavers like the Cross Orbweaver or Marbled Orbweaver. The key is that this species is extraordinarily rare in New England, so any orb weaver you find is statistically much more likely to be one of the common species. Document any potential sighting with detailed photos for expert verification.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents an interesting biogeographical puzzle - primarily known from Texas but with scattered northern records. Climate change may be allowing some southern spider species to expand their ranges northward, making rare sightings like this increasingly important for tracking ecosystem changes.
compareHints: Unlike the abundant Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the variable Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, Araneus bonsallae lacks well-documented field marks for New England populations. Its extreme rarity is actually its most distinguishing feature compared to its common relatives. Any Araneus orb weaver found in New England is far more likely to be one of the established common species than this southwestern rarity.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its cousin the Marbled Orbweaver which has swirled, mottled patterns, the Cross Orbweaver's white cross marking is clean and distinct.

Among New England's Araneus orbweavers, the marbled orbweaver is unique for its extremely inflated, almost spherical abdomen—much rounder than the Cross Orbweaver's more egg-shaped belly or the Shamrock Orbweaver's triangular markings.

Among its Araneus cousins, the barn orbweaver is distinguished by its strong preference for wooden human structures, while the cross orbweaver favors gardens and the marbled orbweaver prefers trees and shrubs.

Among its Araneus cousins, the shamrock orbweaver's white spots make it relatively easy to distinguish - the cross orbweaver has a distinctive white cross pattern, while the marbled orbweaver shows complex marbled coloring without distinct dots.

Nordmann's Orbweaver is generally less distinctively marked than its famous cousins like the Cross Orbweaver (which has a prominent white cross pattern) or the Marbled Orbweaver (with its striking yellow and black marbled appearance).

Among the Araneus orbweavers, the Giant Lichen Orbweaver stands out for its specific lichen-mimicking camouflage, while relatives like the Cross Orbweaver have distinct white cross markings and the Marbled Orbweaver displays smooth, flowing color patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Fierce Orbweaver stands out for its bold behavioral responses rather than distinctive markings like the Cross Orbweaver's white cross or the Marbled Orbweaver's marbled patterns.

Among its Araneus relatives, the Lattice Orbweaver's crosshatch pattern sets it apart from the distinctive white cross of the Cross Orbweaver and the swirled, marble-like patterns of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Unlike the Cross Orbweaver which prefers gardens and woodland edges, or the Marbled Orbweaver found on trees, the Openfield Orbweaver specifically chooses exposed grasslands and meadows.

Among its Araneus relatives in New England, the Red-spotted Orbweaver is most easily distinguished by its reddish markings - the Cross Orbweaver has a white cross pattern, the Marbled Orbweaver has marbled yellow and brown coloring, and the Shamrock Orbweaver has a distinctive shamrock-like pattern.

Among the many Araneus orbweavers in New England, the Butterfly Orbweaver stands out for its wing-like geometric patterns rather than the cross-shaped markings of the Cross Orbweaver or the marble-stone appearance of the Marbled Orbweaver.
Among its many Araneus relatives in New England, the Juniper Orbweaver's defining characteristic is its habitat specialization rather than distinctive markings.

Unlike the Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross pattern on the back, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its orange and white marbled appearance, the White-bellied Orbweaver's key feature is underneath rather than on top.

Among its Araneus cousins in New England, the Red-backed Orbweaver's bright green front section makes it stand out from the typically brown or gray Cross Orbweaver and the yellow-and-black patterned Marbled Orbweaver.
Distinguishing Araneus iviei from its many orbweaver relatives in New England requires expert knowledge, as most species in this genus share similar web-building behavior and general body structure.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its distinctive white cross marking, or the Marbled Orbweaver with its mottled, marbled pattern, the Black-spotted Orbweaver displays clear black spots as its defining feature.

Unlike the common Cross Orbweaver with its white cross markings or the Marbled Orbweaver with its yellow and black patterns, the Humped bog orbweaver's most distinctive feature is its physical shape rather than its coloration.
